176.title: Pauri 7, meaning: fame without grace
176.hook: live four ages and be famous everywhere; without His kindly glance, no one asks after you (Japji 7)
176.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the seventh pauri each morning; it is often quoted in talks on humility and on seva done without seeking praise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri seven, jug, an age. Your line was je jug chaare: if your life lasted all four ages, and ten times more. Today, the turn. Day one hundred seventy-six.

The phone lights up, and there's the count. How many people liked the photo. How many people read your post. Whether anyone noticed the thing you worked so hard on. It's human to want to be seen, and it can sting when you aren't. Now stretch that as far as it goes: famous everywhere on earth, for age upon age. Guru Nanak's seventh pauri imagines exactly that, and then asks one quiet question about it.
screen: `CHECKING THE NUMBERS.` → `FAMOUS EVERYWHERE, FOREVER.` → `ONE QUIET QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. If your life lasted the four ages, and ten times more; if you were known in all nine regions of the world, and everyone walked along with you; if you kept a good name, and won praise and renown across the world: if His kindly glance doesn't fall on you, no one will ask after you. There's that word from pauri four: nadar, the gracious glance. Everything the world admires, long life, fame, followers, a good reputation, is stacked up as high as it can go, and then weighed against one glance, and the glance is heavier. Then the pauri gets sharper. Without that glance, it says, a person is like a worm among worms, and even wrongdoers point fingers at him. Strong words, but they're not an insult to anyone; they're a picture of how small fame really is, in the end. And then comes a turn toward mercy. Nanak, the One gives virtue to those who have none, and gives more virtue to the virtuous. And there's no one, the pauri says, who could give Him any virtue in return. So the whole thing flips. Fame is something the world hands out and takes back. Nadar is something only the Giver gives, freely, even to people who have nothing to show. The pauri doesn't call praise wicked. Being thanked is lovely. It just says fame isn't it: not the thing that lasts, and not the thing that decides whether anyone asks after you.
screen: `FAMOUS IN ALL NINE REGIONS.` · `WITHOUT THE GLANCE, NO ONE ASKS.` · `A WORM AMONG WORMS.` · `VIRTUE GIVEN TO THE VIRTUELESS.` · then, large: `FAME IS NOT IT.`

segments.voice: Sit easily, and think of one place where you want to be praised right now. A post, a project, a family argument you want to be seen winning. Notice how it feels in your body: a small leaning forward, a waiting. Now, just for this bell, let the leaning go. Sit back. Imagine that no one ever finds out how good that thing was, and see what's left. Maybe there's still something good in it. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Nadar. The kindly glance: without it, even a life famous for four ages and more means no one asks after you.
Your line: fame is not it. Today, do one good thing and don't mention it to anyone, not even a hint. Day one hundred seventy-six.

177.title: Pauri 8, sound: suniai
177.tomorrow: Pauri 8, meaning: the power of listening
177.howItsDone: Pauris eight to eleven of Japji, each line beginning suniai, are part of the morning recitation; together they are Japji's stretch on listening to the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nadar, and the turn of pauri seven: famous for ages, and still, without the glance, no one asks after you. Your line was fame is not it. Did one good thing go unmentioned? Day one hundred seventy-seven.

Back at the start of this camp, on Japji Sahib, we said Japji would give four whole pauris to one word. Today is the day that word arrives. It's a soft word, almost a sigh, and once you've heard it you'll hear it all through this part of Japji, because for four pauris straight it starts nearly every line. If you've ever sat in a gurdwara at dawn while Japji is recited, this is the stretch where the word rolls around and around the room like a wave coming in.
screen: `FOUR PAURIS FOR ONE WORD.` → `A SOFT WORD, ALMOST A SIGH.` → `A WAVE COMING IN.`

segments.voice: The word is suniai. Let's sound it: SUN-i-ai. The first syllable is like soon, but short, closer to the u in put. Then a light i. Then ai, a little like the start of air. Sun-i-ai. The n in the middle, in Gurmukhi, is the one made with the tongue curled back, the same n you heard at the end of taan in pauri three. Suniai comes from sunnaa, to hear, to listen, and the ending means something like by, or through. So: by listening. Through hearing. The opening line of pauri eight: suniai sidh peer sur naath. Sidh: siddhas, yogis said to have gained great powers. Peer: pirs, the Sufi masters, the spiritual guides of Muslim Punjab. Sur: the gods. Naath: the naths, masters of a yogic order; the stories of Guru Nanak's travels have him meeting and talking with them. So in one breath the line names holy people of many kinds from Guru Nanak's world, and says they came to be what they are by listening. Now listen to the rhythm of the whole stretch. Pauri eight: suniai, suniai, suniai, suniai. Pauri nine, the same. Pauri ten, the same. Pauri eleven, the same. Line after line opening on the same soft word. Japji keeps that drumbeat going for four whole pauris. And every one of these four pauris ends on the same two lines, a refrain about devotees being always in bloom. We'll open all of that tomorrow. For today, one word is enough. Suniai. By listening.
screen: `SUNIAI — BY LISTENING.` · `SIDH, PEER, SUR, NAATH.` · `HOLY PEOPLE OF MANY KINDS.` · `FOUR PAURIS, ONE DRUMBEAT.` · then, large: `SUNIAI.`

segments.voice: Say the word slowly, five times, with a breath between each one. Suniai. Breathe. Suniai. Breathe. Suniai. Breathe. Suniai. Breathe. Suniai. Now stop speaking, and do what the word says. Listen. The room, the street, your own breath, the small hum of whatever machine is nearby. Don't name anything. Just receive it. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the last sound before the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Suniai. By listening. The soft word that opens nearly every line of Japji's pauris eight to eleven.
Your line: suniai, listening. Today, in one conversation, let the other person finish completely before you start. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

178.title: Pauri 8, meaning: the power of listening
178.hook: by listening one becomes a sage, knows earth and sky, and death cannot touch the devotee (Japji 8)
178.tomorrow: Pauri 9: listening, the gods and scriptures
178.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the eighth pauri each morning; its refrain, that by listening pain and wrongdoing are wiped away, is why listening to Gurbani, in kirtan or katha, is itself treated as practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the soft word: suniai. Your line was suniai, listening. Did you let someone finish completely before you spoke? Day one hundred seventy-eight.

The best listeners aren't always the ones with the best advice. They're the ones who actually stop when someone talks. Phone face down. No answer being planned while the other person is still speaking. A conversation like that can feel like being let into a room you forgot you had. Listening like that changes people. Guru Nanak's eighth pauri makes a much bigger claim about it: listening doesn't just change people. It reaches all the way to earth and sky.
screen: `THE ONE WHO ACTUALLY STOPS.` → `THE PHONE, FACE DOWN.` → `LISTENING REACHES EARTH AND SKY.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. By listening, people become siddhas, pirs, gods and masters of yoga. By listening, the earth, the bull that is said to hold it up, and the sky. By listening, the continents, the worlds and the regions below. By listening, death cannot touch you. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. Listening to what? Sikh commentators answer: to the Name, to the shabad, the Guru's word. Suniai isn't just hearing noise; it's taking in the true Name until it rearranges you. Notice how the pauri moves. It starts with holy people. Then it gets huge: earth, sky, the old picture of the bull beneath the world, whole continents and underworlds. It's as if the pauri is saying that listening is not a small, private hobby; it's how things come to understand their place in everything. Later in Japji, Guru Nanak will gently reinterpret that bull, but that's for another day. Then the pauri comes close again, to one person: death can't touch you. Poh na sakai kaal. Kaal is death, and time; the fear of it loses its grip. And the refrain: Naanak bhagtaa sadaa vigaas. Vigaas is the same flower word you met in pauri three, vigsai, blossoming. The devotees are always opening, like flowers. Suniai dookh paap kaa naas: by listening, pain and wrongdoing are destroyed. That's a big promise for something as quiet as listening, and the same two lines will close each of the next three pauris.
screen: `SAGES AND MASTERS, BY LISTENING.` · `EARTH, BULL AND SKY.` · `DEATH CANNOT TOUCH.` · `VIGAAS — ALWAYS IN BLOOM.` · then, large: `BY LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is for later, with a person. Right now, get ready for it. Think of one person you'll talk to today. Picture yourself with them, phone face down, turned toward them. Decide now: you'll listen fully, without planning your reply, and ask one more question before you say anything about yourself. Hold that intention. Then, for the rest of the bell, practice on the world: just listen to whatever is here. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Suniai. By listening: sages, earth and sky; by listening, death cannot touch, and devotees are always in bloom.
Your line: by listening. Listen fully to one person today, and ask one more question before you talk about yourself. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

179.title: Pauri 9: listening, the gods and scriptures
179.hook: suniai: by listening even the lowly speak praise, and the scriptures open (Japji 9)
179.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the ninth pauri each morning as part of Japji's four suniai pauris; each ends with the same refrain, that devotees are always in bloom and listening wipes away pain and wrongdoing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, suniai, and the power of listening. Your line was by listening. Did someone get your full attention, and one more question? Day one hundred seventy-nine.

There's the cynic at work who never has a kind word. The uncle who complains through every holiday, every single year. And then, sometimes, something shifts, a loss, a friendship, maybe just time, and one day a generous sentence comes out of that same mouth, and the whole table goes quiet. Where did that come from? This week's stretch of Japji, pauris nine to fifteen, is about listening and then trusting. And pauri nine, the second listening stanza, has an answer for that uncle.
screen: `THE ONE WHO COMPLAINED.` → `ONE DAY, SOMETHING GENEROUS.` → `WHERE DID THAT COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Pauri nine keeps yesterday's drumbeat, suniai, by listening, at the start of every line. Here it is in plain words, following Macauliffe. By listening, Shiva, Brahma and Indra. By listening, even the lowly and the foul-mouthed come to praise. By listening, the ways of yoga and the secrets of the body. By listening, the Shastras, the Smritis and the Vedas. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. Start with the first line. Shiva, Brahma and Indra are great gods in Hindu tradition, and Guru Nanak names them with respect. The pauri places even their greatness inside listening to the Name. Sikh commentators read this as saying that the One is the source, and all greatness, however high, comes by hearing. Then this: suniai mukh saalaahan mand. Mand means the low, the bad; mukh is the mouth. By listening, even those with bad mouths praise. On this reading, nobody is too far gone. Listening, the pauri says, can turn the most bitter tongue toward praise. Then the body: jog jugat tan bhed, the methods of yoga and the hidden workings of the body. And then the scriptures of Guru Nanak's world: Shastras, Smritis, Vedas. By listening, they open. Their meaning isn't locked in the letters; it comes to the one who listens. So this pauri moves from gods, to the worst mouth in the room, to the body, to the books, and says the same thing about each. Whatever is high, whatever is low: the door is listening.
screen: `SHIVA, BRAHMA, INDRA — BY LISTENING.` · `MAND — EVEN THE BAD MOUTH PRAISES.` · `THE BODY'S HIDDEN WAYS.` · `THE SCRIPTURES OPEN.` · then, large: `THE LOWLY SPEAK PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and listen for three sounds around you. The first one, the loudest: name it quietly. The second, softer, something you'd missed until now. And the third, the faintest you can find: a hum, a breath, the air itself. Stay with that third one. Notice how much more you hear when you're looking for it. Then think of one person whose voice you've stopped listening to, and imagine hearing them freshly. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Mand. The low, the bad: even the bad-mouthed, by listening, come to praise, along with the gods, the body's secrets and the scriptures.
Your line: the lowly speak praise. Today, when someone you've written off says something good, hear it, and tell them you heard it. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

180.title: Pauri 10: listening, truth and contentment
180.hook: suniai: by listening come truth, contentment and wisdom, worth bathing at every shrine (Japji 10)
180.tomorrow: Pauri 11: listening, the blind find the way
180.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the tenth pauri each morning; santokh, contentment, is often taught as one of five virtues, with sat (truth), daya (compassion), nimrata (humility) and pyaar (love).

segments.voice: Yesterday, mand, the low: by listening, even the bad-mouthed turn to praise. Your line was the lowly speak praise. Did you hear something good from someone unexpected? Day one hundred eighty.

There's a moment most of us know. You're scrolling through something you might buy, a jacket, a phone, a trip, and you already have one that works perfectly well. You know it. And still there's a little tug: but this one's better. The tug never quite goes away; there's always a next one. Now think of the rare moments when the tug stops. A meal with friends where nobody checks the time. A quiet evening when nothing is missing. Pauri ten has a name for that feeling, and says where it comes from.
screen: `BUT THIS ONE'S BETTER.` → `THE TUG THAT NEVER STOPS.` → `WHEN NOTHING IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: Here is pauri ten in plain words, following Macauliffe. By listening come truth, contentment and divine knowledge. By listening, the bath at the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage. By listening, reading and reading, honor is won. By listening, the mind settles easily into meditation. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. The first line is the heart of it: suniai sat santokh giaan. Sat is truth, the same root as sach. Giaan is knowledge, wisdom. And in the middle, today's word: santokh. Contentment. Enough. Not giving up, not pretending not to want anything. It's the settled feeling of having enough, the tug gone quiet. Sikh teaching often counts santokh among the great virtues, alongside truth, compassion, humility and love. Notice where the pauri says it comes from: listening. Not from getting the next thing, and not from grimly denying yourself. From hearing the Name until the restless wanting loosens its grip on its own. Then that second line: the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage. Indian tradition counted sixty-eight great bathing places, and people walked for months to reach them. Remember pauri six, the bath that's only worth it if it pleases Him. Here Guru Nanak says it plainly: listening is the bath at all sixty-eight at once. And the last line before the refrain: sahaj dhiaan. Sahaj is ease, naturalness. The meditation that comes without forcing. Contentment and ease, by listening. You don't have to wrestle the tug down. You listen, and it quiets.
screen: `SAT, SANTOKH, GIAAN.` · `SANTOKH — ENOUGH.` · `THE SIXTY-EIGHT SHRINES AT ONCE.` · `SAHAJ — MEDITATION WITH EASE.` · then, large: `ENOUGH, BY LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing in front of you, or in your life, exactly as it is. Your chair. Your hands. The light in the room. This day, as it's gone so far. Don't improve it in your head. Don't compare it to a better version. Just let it be enough, for the length of the bell. When the tug comes, and it will, notice it, and go back to listening: to your breath, to the room. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Santokh. Contentment, the settled sense of enough. Japji's tenth pauri says it comes by listening.
Your line: enough, by listening. The next time you feel the tug to buy or add something today, wait one full minute and just listen to what's around you. Day one hundred eighty.

181.title: Pauri 11: listening, the blind find the way
181.hook: suniai: by listening the blind find the path and the unfathomable becomes clear (Japji 11)
181.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib every morning as part of Nitnem; Pauri 11 is the last of the four stanzas that begin suniai, by listening, and each of those four ends with the same refrain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 10 and santokh, contentment. Your line was enough, by listening. Was there one thing you let be enough, just as it was? Today, the last of the four listening stanzas. Day one hundred eighty-one.

The power goes out at night. The screen dies, the room goes black, and for a second you're lost in your own home. Then you start listening. The fridge is silent, so the kitchen is there. The clock ticks on the left. A car passes, so the window is ahead. Without planning to, you've made a map out of sound, and you find the door. Someone who lives without sight may do this with far more skill, reading a street by its echoes. Japji has been saying suniai, by listening, for three stanzas. Today it reaches for the picture of finding your way in the dark.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `A MAP MADE OF SOUND.` → `SUNIAI, ONE LAST TIME.`

segments.voice: Pauri 11 is the fourth and last of the suniai stanzas, and like the others it's a string of short lines, each starting with the same word. Here is its central line in Guru Nanak's own words: suniai andhe paavahi raahu. By listening, the blind find the road. Around it, in paraphrase: by listening, a person dives deep into oceans of virtue. By listening, ordinary people become like the shaikhs, the pirs and the kings. And then the line that answers today's hook: by listening, what was fathomless comes within your hand. The word there is asagaah, water too deep to wade across. Listening doesn't drain the ocean. It puts the far shore in reach. So who are the blind? Sikh commentators read this as a blindness anyone can have: not knowing which way to go, stumbling around in our own ego. It isn't a promise about eyes, and it isn't a remark about people who can't see. The picture is the one from the power cut. When you can't see the way, you can still hear it. And what are we listening to? In Japji, it's the Name and the Guru's word, the shabad. The listening is what turns into direction. Then every suniai stanza closes the same way, and this is the last time we'll hear it for a while: Nanak says the devotees are always in bloom, and by listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. Four stanzas, one lesson. Before you can trust, before you can walk, you listen.
screen: `SUNIAI ANDHE PAAVAHI RAAHU.` · `THE UNWADEABLE COMES WITHIN REACH.` · `A BLINDNESS ANYONE CAN HAVE.` · `LISTENING BECOMES DIRECTION.` · then, large: `THE BLIND FIND THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen, for as long as the bell allows. Don't name the sounds at first. Just let them arrive. Then, slowly, let them make a map: what's near, what's far, what's to your left, what's behind you. Notice how much of the room you can find without looking. If a thought pulls you away, come back by finding where one sound is coming from. The bell holds the time.
Asagaah. Fathomless, water too deep to wade across: by listening, it comes within reach, and the blind find the road.
Your line: the blind find the way. Today, when you don't know what to do next, stop looking for a moment and listen: to the room, to a friend, to the quiet. Day one hundred eighty-one.

182.title: Pauri 12, sound: mannai
182.hook: mannai kee gat kahee na jaae
182.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; pauris 12 to 15 each begin with mannai, and the move from suniai, listening, to mannai, trusting, is often taught as steps on one path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asagaah, the fathomless, and the last listening stanza. Your line was the blind find the way. Did listening show you a way when looking didn't? Today, a new word takes over. Day one hundred eighty-two.

It's the end of a week, so look back at the road. Pauri 7 told us fame is not it. Then came suniai, by listening, and four stanzas of it: the power of listening, the lowly singing praise, santokh, enough, and yesterday the blind finding the way. That's a whole week of ears. Hearing advice and taking it are two different things. Your friend says, get some sleep, and you hear it, and you stay up anyway. Hearing is the first step. Something else has to happen for the words to move in. Japji knows this. Today it changes its word.
screen: `A WEEK OF LISTENING.` → `HEARING ADVICE, TAKING IT.` → `A NEW WORD.`

segments.voice: The new word is mannai. Say it with the n held a moment: MUN-nai. It comes from the Punjabi verb mannanaa, and that verb is wide. It means to accept, to agree, to obey, to believe, to trust, to take something to heart. When a Punjabi mother tells a child, gall mann lai, she means take my word, go along with it. In Japji, mannai means by trusting, by taking the Word to heart. For the next four stanzas, pauris 12 to 15, line after line begins with it, the way the last four began with suniai. Listen to the first line of Pauri 12 in the original: mannai kee gat kahee na jaae. Mannai kee, of the one who trusts. Gat, the state, the condition someone is in. Kahee na jaae, cannot be told. The state of the one who trusts cannot be put into words. Hear the rhythm: mannai kee gat, three quick beats, then kahee na jaae, slowing down, as if the sentence itself runs out of breath. Tomorrow we'll open what it means. Today is for the sound. And notice the order Guru Nanak chose. First suniai, listening. Then mannai, trusting. One way Sikh teachers describe the path: you hear the Word, then you take it in, then you live it. Suniai, then mannai: a word goes in the ear, then it goes home.
screen: `MANNAI — BY TRUSTING.` · `ACCEPT, OBEY, TAKE TO HEART.` · `MANNAI KEE GAT KAHEE NA JAAE.` · `FIRST LISTEN, THEN TRUST.` · then, large: `MANNAI.`

segments.voice: Say mannai slowly, five times. Let each one take a full breath out: MUN-nai. Hold the n, then let the ending open. Between each, rest in the quiet for a few breaths. If it helps, think of one thing you've heard and haven't yet taken to heart, and let the word sit beside it. Then just sit, breathing, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mannai. By trusting, by taking the Word to heart. It opens line after line of pauris 12 to 15, after four stanzas of listening.
Your line: mannai, trusting. Today, take one piece of good advice you've already heard, and actually follow it, once. Day one hundred eighty-two.
